newsitem.title: USA: Mrs. Clinton seeks child development support.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton seeks child development support.

text.p: First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton said Monday any increased spending for early childhood development programmes would be offset by the need for fewer prisons and drug treatment centres.

Mrs. Clinton, who along with President Clinton Thursday hosts a White House conference on early childhood development, promoted broad-based efforts to aid infants and youngsters, including those of parents and local community groups, as well as federal and state governments.
"We have moved considerably from the idea that top down, one size fits all solutions are the way we should go," Mrs. Clinton told a small group of reporters at the White House.

"But we have not yet really accepted, I think, the evidence that is around us that there are many strategies that do work, that if we spent a little money and a little time implimenting, would have big payoffs," she said.

Discussing federal research data that shows the long-term benefits of stimulating a child's learning skills before they reach the age of three, Mrs. Clinton cited the achievements of early Head Start programmes and some day care centres.

She chided critics who oppose any federal involvement on the grounds "its too expensive, its too interventionist and it won't work, and that what we need to do is get back to a time when each individual was responsible for him or herself."
"We are all in this together, whether we like it or not," she said, adding that "what we want to do is sort of increase the odds" that all youngsters succeed.

"We just have to acknowledge that there are certain kinds of investments that will save us money," she said. "If we invested on the front end of some of these early intervention strategies, I honestly believe that we would not be spending so much money on prisons and mental health and drug abuse treatment."

Asked if she would like to see paid maternity leave for new mothers, similar to programmes now common in Europe, Mrs. Clinton replied: "Of course I'd be for it if it were feasible, if it were economically and politically feasible."

"I don't know what the terms or ... the specifics of it would be, but I think it is the kind of policy that would make it possible for many more parents to take time to become attached to their child early on," she said.

Stressing that she was "speaking just personally, not for the administration or anybody else" on maternity leave, the first lady said she did not see any realistic chance it would be enacted by Congress.
"People believe that in our current political climate and given the sort of characteristics that mark the American political character that it is not realistic," she said.
